text: The t-test is the everyday tool for comparing averages. Is our delivery time really different from the promise we make? Do desktop shoppers spend more than mobile shoppers? Did a loyalty program change what the same customers spend? Those three questions map onto the three flavors of t-test. This lesson is about choosing the right version and reading the output correctly.

A t statistic is a signal-to-noise ratio — the observed difference divided by its standard error. If the null is true, the t statistic follows the t distribution, a bell shape with slightly heavier tails than normal, accounting for the extra uncertainty of estimating spread from a small sample. A large absolute t means the difference is big relative to its noise.

First, the one-sample t-test — comparing one group's mean to a fixed value. We promise 3.0-day delivery and observe 25 deliveries averaging 3.38 days. The test gives t equals 2.055, p equals 0.0509 — just above 0.05. That doesn't mean delivery matches the promise; it means this particular sample doesn't quite clear the bar. The line between 0.049 and 0.051 is arbitrary, which is why you report the estimate and its uncertainty, not just a verdict.

Second, the two-sample t-test for independent groups — comparing desktop versus mobile order values. The gap is 7.91 dollars, with t equals 2.3 and p equals 0.0246 using Welch's version, which doesn't assume equal variances between groups. The classic Student version gives a different answer, 2.461 and p equals 0.0155, on the exact same data — which is why the choice matters when group sizes and variances differ.

To describe how big the gap is, use an effect size like Cohen's d — the mean difference in pooled standard deviations. Here it comes to about 0.49, a medium-sized effect by common rules of thumb: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large, though treat these as rough labels, not rules.

Third, the paired t-test — when each row in one group is matched to a row in the other, like the same customers before and after a loyalty program. It analyzes the per-customer differences directly, and here it finds a clear effect, p equals 0.0011.

Treating that very same data as two independent groups instead gives p equals 0.2509 and misses the effect entirely, because customer-to-customer spending differences drown out the real change. Pairing removes that variation. Using the right test for how the data was actually collected is more than a technicality.

By default, scipy runs two-sided tests, where the mean could be higher or lower. Pass alternative equals greater or less for a one-sided test, but only if you decided on that direction before seeing the data and would truly ignore an effect in the other direction. When in doubt, stay two-sided.

Three assumptions to check: independence, that observations aren't influenced by each other except in a deliberate paired design; roughly normal data or a decent sample size, since the central limit theorem makes the t-test fairly robust, though very small samples with heavy skew call for a permutation or rank-based test instead; and random assignment or sampling, since the test can't fix a biased sample.

To recap: the t-test compares means as a signal-to-noise ratio. Use one-sample against a fixed value, Welch's two-sample for independent groups, and paired for matched measurements. Always report the difference, an effect size, and the p-value — never just a bare significant or not. Next, when the outcome is a category rather than a number: the chi-square test.
